question: At fixed context exposure, why do neural next-token predictors fit broad target distributions less accurately than concentrated ones, and can the dependence on ambiguity be decomposed into capacity, representation dimension, optimization time, and label-sampling noise?

key_findings.claim: In the paper's random-association linear-head model, storing a uniform size-k next-token distribution consumes approximately k times the capacity of storing a deterministic association.
key_findings.evidence: A Hebbian outer-product construction decomposes logits into target signal and cross-context interference whose per-coordinate variance scales as nk/(hd). Keeping interference below signal gives capacity proportional to hd/k, up to logarithmic factors. A sign-pattern argument supplies a matching upper scaling for any linear-softmax model, and Adam experiments recover the hd and inverse-k trends.

key_findings.claim: Even an ideal backbone needs output embedding dimension that grows linearly with support size to represent every possible size-k target support.
key_findings.evidence: Through a k-neighborly-polytope construction, the paper states an exact-representation threshold h>=2k for all size-k supports under optimally chosen embeddings. With context-dependent embedding perturbations, a compressed-sensing construction adds a logarithmic factor in d/k while retaining linear dependence on k.

key_findings.claim: Ambiguity slows early expected-loss optimization and leaves a larger finite-time error even after all support sizes enter the same 1/t asymptotic rate.
key_findings.evidence: For one context under gradient flow, the on/off-support logit gap reduces to a scalar implicit equation. At small time, KL is approximately log(d/k)-t/k, so its initial improvement rate is 1/k. At large time, KL is approximately k(d-k)/(td), yielding the same 1/t rate but a roughly k-proportional prefactor when k is much smaller than d.

key_findings.claim: One-hot next-token sampling adds a k-dependent within-support noise floor that is absent for deterministic targets in the leading-order stochastic-differential approximation.
key_findings.evidence: Sampling scatters on-support logits while leaving their leading-order mean trajectory unchanged. The stationary second-order KL excess is (k-1)/(4k), equal to zero for k=1 and approaching 1/4 as k grows. The text cautions that finite-step discrete SGD can also slow the mean rate beyond this small-step approximation.

key_findings.claim: A small transformer trained on a controlled word-level 3-gram process shows the predicted ambiguity signature and primarily fails by assigning mass outside the true support.
key_findings.evidence: The default four-layer, four-head, 4M-parameter transformer is trained for 3,000 steps on about 98M sampled tokens from 1.1M empirical TinyStories contexts. At a fixed context-frequency bin, KL rises and on-support mass falls with effective support size. Increasing backbone width or duration mostly shifts an iso-loss contour, whereas increasing head embedding dimension or optimizing full KL instead of sampled cross-entropy disproportionately improves high-support contexts.

key_findings.claim: OLMo-2 1B disagrees more with OLMo-2 13B on higher-ambiguity natural contexts at fixed estimated semantic frequency, but this is a proxy-on-proxy observational result rather than ground-truth distribution error.
key_findings.evidence: On 100,000 Dolma sequences of length 512, OLMo-2 13B supplies both the reference next-token distribution and embeddings for a nearest-neighbor density estimate; OLMo-2 1B supplies the evaluated distribution. Within semantic-frequency bins, log KL correlates with log effective support at about r=0.61 and with raw support at about r=0.83. The reference model is itself imperfect and the density proxy is noisy in the rare tail.

key_findings.claim: Natural-data structure creates a major exception to frequency-only predictions: rare contexts can be easy when in-context copying supplies a reusable algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: In the low-frequency, low-loss band, 61% of next tokens match an earlier in-context bigram continuation versus 11.2% elsewhere; 33% match a trigram continuation versus 3.4% elsewhere. On the synthetic 3-gram task, the density proxy correlates well when positions are frequency-weighted (Pearson 0.86, Spearman 0.92) but poorly across unique contexts (0.30 and 0.24), exposing rare-context noise.

method.core_idea: Model ambiguity as the effective number of plausible next tokens and isolate four mechanisms by which it raises error: associative-memory interference, output-dimension expressivity, cross-entropy optimization dynamics, and stochastic one-hot label noise; then seek the same signatures in controlled transformers and pretrained language models.
method.mechanism: The theoretical target is uniform on a random support of size k in vocabulary d. With random unit context embeddings, a Hebbian linear head yields a capacity law; with learned ideal embeddings, convex-polytope and compressed-sensing results yield dimension thresholds. One-context gradient flow reduces to the logit gap between on- and off-support tokens. A stochastic differential equation adds sampled-label perturbations and tracks within-support logit variance. Experiments train a four-layer transformer on an empirical TinyStories 3-gram generator while varying residual width, output embedding width, steps, and sampled versus distributional loss. For natural text, OLMo-2 13B serves as a reference distribution and embedding-density estimator, and OLMo-2 1B/7B disagreement is analyzed by estimated ambiguity and semantic context frequency.
assumptions: Ambiguity can be summarized by support size for uniform targets or exp(entropy) for non-uniform targets.
Random supports and random nearly orthogonal context embeddings are useful approximations for deriving linear-head capacity.
A linear output head captures a central bottleneck even though a trained transformer backbone can share structure across contexts and adapt its representations.
The Hebbian construction is representative enough to expose capacity scaling, while the separate sign-pattern bound controls what any linear-softmax head can store.
Gradient flow and a small-step stochastic differential equation approximate the relevant phases of practical AdamW/SGD training.
OLMo-2 13B is closer to the unknown natural next-token distribution than OLMo-2 1B, and its last-layer embedding density is a meaningful proxy for semantic context exposure.
Holding estimated context frequency fixed removes enough exposure variation to interpret remaining loss trends as ambiguity effects.

techniques.role: Uses uniform random size-k supports to vary distributional ambiguity independently of vocabulary and context count.
Separates desired logits from cross-pattern interference to derive the hd/k storage law.
Relates exact representation of every top-k support to convex-polytope neighborliness and the h>=2k threshold.
Constructs approximately correct predictions under perturbed embeddings with dimension linear in k up to a log(d/k) factor.
Collapses symmetric on/off-support optimization to one logit-gap trajectory and extracts early- and late-time rates.
Models one-hot next-token sampling as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck perturbation and derives within-support variance and a KL floor.
Summarizes per-context transformer loss across frequency and effective support to distinguish shifts from ambiguity-specific rotations.
Uses PCA-reduced OLMo embeddings and FAISS nearest-neighbor kernels to approximate how often semantically similar natural contexts occur.

evaluations.metric: Number of size-k context distributions stored at fixed error
evaluations.result: Capacity proportional to h*d/k up to logarithmic factors
evaluations.baseline: k=1 deterministic associations use roughly one kth of the capacity per context

evaluations.setting: Ideal and perturbed backbone representation theory
evaluations.result: Exact universal support representation at h>=2k; robust construction remains linear in k with an added log(d/k) factor
evaluations.baseline: General softmax-bottleneck bounds depend on vocabulary/rank rather than target support size

evaluations.result: Early KL approximately log(d/k)-t/k; late KL approximately k(d-k)/(td)
evaluations.baseline: Lower-k targets learn faster and have smaller finite-time prefactors

evaluations.metric: Asymptotic KL excess over expected-loss gradient flow
evaluations.baseline: Zero at k=1 and approaches 0.25 as k grows

evaluations.setting: TinyStories-derived 3-gram generator; default 4-layer 4M transformer; about 98M training tokens
evaluations.metric: Per-context KL, support mass, and entropy gap
evaluations.result: At fixed context frequency, loss and off-support mass increase with effective support size
evaluations.baseline: Capacity/duration give mostly uniform contour shifts; embedding width/full-distribution loss preferentially improve ambiguous contexts

evaluations.setting: OLMo-2 1B evaluated against OLMo-2 13B on 51.2M Dolma positions
evaluations.metric: Within-frequency correlation between log KL and log ambiguity
evaluations.result: Approximately r=0.61 for effective support and r=0.83 for raw support
evaluations.baseline: OLMo-2 7B reduces KL overall but remains evaluated against the same 13B proxy

evaluations.setting: Semantic-frequency proxy validation on the synthetic 3-gram task
evaluations.metric: Correlation with true log context frequency
evaluations.baseline: Across distinct contexts, correlations fall to 0.30 and 0.24 because the rare tail is noisy

limitations: Author-stated: the theory uses uniform random supports and largely unstructured context associations, whereas natural language shares compositional mechanisms across contexts.

Author-stated: the main analytical object is the linear head with fixed or idealized embeddings; backbone representation learning is treated as secondary and can short-circuit memorization through structure.
Author-stated: OLMo-2 13B is not the true natural-text distribution, and embedding distance is only a coarse, biased frequency proxy.
Author-stated: the semantic-frequency estimate is least reliable for rare and early-sequence contexts; its strong synthetic correlation is dominated by frequently occurring positions.

Reviewer-identified: the closely related uncited paper Next-Token Prediction Should be Ambiguity-Sensitive (arXiv:2506.16288) already reports that transformers struggle under high latent-task ambiguity across scales and proposes ambiguity-adaptive Monte Carlo prediction. The present paper's novelty is therefore its four-root quantitative theory and natural-token evidence, not first identifying ambiguity-dependent prediction difficulty.

Reviewer-identified: Distribution Prompting (arXiv:2505.12244) finds very low- and very high-entropy targets easier to elicit than moderate-entropy random targets, showing that monotonic difficulty is not universal across target families or tasks; learning empirical supports at fixed frequency and prompt-eliciting arbitrary distributions are different problems that should be explicitly reconciled.

Reviewer-identified: the synthetic transformer ablations use one data seed per configuration and choose the best learning rate for each sweep; uncertainty across datasets, optimization seeds, and tokenizers is not reported.

Reviewer-identified: the natural experiment compares models from one family on their own pretraining corpus, so size changes capacity, representation quality, training compute, and quality of the putative target simultaneously.

Reviewer-identified: no large-model intervention independently varies true ambiguity at matched semantics and exposure, and no experiment shows that the measured distribution error causes failures in sampling, synthetic-data training, inference-time search, or RL exploration.
Reviewer-identified: effective support depends on tokenizer granularity and reference calibration; equivalent semantic uncertainty can be distributed over different numbers of tokens.
failure_modes: Shared linguistic structure, synonym classes, induction heads, or retrieval can let a rare ambiguous context reuse a learned mechanism and violate the independent-association capacity model.
A larger reference model can be confidently wrong or differently calibrated, making lower student–teacher KL look like better ground-truth modeling when it is merely closer imitation.
Semantic nearest-neighbor density can confound frequency with representation geometry, position, domain, and the reference model's own inductive bias.
At or above the head's capacity limit, cross-context interference invalidates the decoupled one-context optimization dynamics.
Finite learning rates, minibatch context noise, Adam adaptation, and backbone updates can alter the SDE's predicted mean path and noise floor.
Entropy alone cannot distinguish several coherent modes from diffuse noise; two distributions with equal effective support may differ greatly in geometric representability.
Increasing output dimension beyond the backbone width cannot add usable representational rank, as the paper's d_embed=512/1024 ablation at d_model=256 itself illustrates.
reusable_insights: Stratify language-model error by both exposure and target entropy; aggregate perplexity hides systematically underfit high-ambiguity contexts.
Separate four resource bottlenecks—parameter capacity, output rank, optimization time, and sampled-label variance—because scaling one does not necessarily repair the others.
Compare sampled cross-entropy with distributional supervision in controlled generators to isolate noise caused by observing one continuation per context occurrence.
Inspect off-support mass and entropy gap in addition to KL to learn whether an underfit distribution collapses modes or leaks probability into implausible tokens.
Validate a learned frequency proxy on a domain with known counts and report both occurrence-weighted and unique-context performance.
Treat algorithmic reuse such as in-context copying as a structured exception, not noise to be discarded; it reveals how models escape memorization-based limits.
Allocate model dimension or test-time computation based on estimated ambiguity if high-support contexts are the intended fidelity bottleneck.
open_questions: Can true next-token ambiguity be manipulated at matched semantics, frequency, and tokenizer while training larger transformers to causally test all four predicted roots?
How do support geometry, semantic relatedness, and mode clustering refine the scalar effective-support measure?
Can ambiguity-adaptive output heads, mixture-of-softmax layers, or Monte Carlo predictors overcome the h>=2k and sampling bottlenecks at fixed compute?
Does underfitting high-ambiguity distributions measurably reduce best-of-N inference, on-policy RL exploration, or synthetic-data diversity downstream?
How does the curse transform under subword versus byte tokenization, multi-token prediction, diffusion language modeling, or retrieval augmentation?
What is the capacity law when context representations and output embeddings are trained jointly on structured compositional data rather than random supports?
Can an exposure estimator separate corpus frequency from structural generalization, in-context copying, and memorization for rare natural contexts?
Does fine-tuning on a distribution far from pretraining amplify ambiguity-specific error, as the discussion predicts?

competitive_landscape.title: Next-Token Prediction Should be Ambiguity-Sensitive: A Meta-Learning Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: MetaHMM already shows that transformers underperform a Bayesian oracle when the posterior over latent sequence tasks is broad and proposes a test-time scalable Monte Carlo predictor. Curse of Ambiguity studies aleatoric breadth of the next-token target itself, derives explicit capacity/dimension/optimization/noise scalings, and adds natural-language evidence, but it does not propose or test a mitigation.

competitive_landscape.title: Distribution Prompting: Understanding the Expressivity of Language Models Through the Next-Token Distributions They Can Produce
competitive_landscape.difference: Distribution Prompting optimizes prompts to elicit arbitrary target distributions from a fixed model and finds a non-monotonic entropy effect: low- and high-entropy targets can be easier than moderate ones, with geometry and LM-origin targets mattering. Curse of Ambiguity instead studies learning empirical conditional distributions at matched exposure and random-support theory; the differing results show entropy is not a universal one-dimensional difficulty ordering.

competitive_landscape.title: Softmax Bottleneck Makes Language Models Unable to Represent Multi-mode Word Distributions
competitive_landscape.difference: Chang and McCallum show geometrically that one hidden state cannot elevate several appropriate word modes without also elevating interfering embeddings, and propose multi-facet softmax. The new paper sharpens one aspect into a universal h>=2k support-size threshold and combines it with capacity, optimization, and sampling analyses.

competitive_landscape.title: Breaking the Softmax Bottleneck: A High-Rank RNN Language Model
competitive_landscape.difference: The softmax-bottleneck work frames language modeling as low-rank matrix factorization and uses a mixture of softmaxes to increase output rank. Curse of Ambiguity conditions the required rank and storage on target support size and adds finite-time and stochastic-learning mechanisms rather than a new output architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Associative Memories
competitive_landscape.difference: Scaling Laws for Associative Memories derives parameter/sample scaling for outer-product memory models of context–label associations. Curse of Ambiguity adopts this Hebbian lens but makes each context map to k plausible labels and isolates the resulting inverse-k capacity dependence.

competitive_landscape.title: Tracing LLM Behavior to the Training Data with Empirical Next-Token Distributions
competitive_landscape.difference: Tracing LLM Behavior directly compares model predictions with empirical next-token distributions where training-data contexts can be counted, finding agreement improves with scale but has a long error tail. Curse of Ambiguity provides a mechanistic support-size theory and a much larger natural analysis, but uses OLMo-13B and embedding density proxies instead of empirical distributions for long contexts.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: the paper identifies and formalizes a curse of ambiguity and traces it to four roots—capacity proportional to 1/k, embedding dimension at least 2k, slower/higher finite-time optimization error, and a sampled-label noise floor—then observes matching signatures in transformers and OLMo. Reviewer inference after primary-work comparison: the broad phenomenon that high ambiguity strains transformer prediction is not new; arXiv:2506.16288 states it directly in a latent-task setting, and softmax-bottleneck papers already analyze multimodal output restrictions. The defensible novelty is the unusually unified quantitative decomposition by next-token support size, especially the combined hd/k capacity law, neighborliness threshold, explicit gradient-flow regimes, label-noise floor, and aligned synthetic-to-natural diagnostic. Claims should be framed as a new theory and synthesis of ambiguity costs, not the first observation that ambiguous predictions are hard.
reviewer_notes: The 58-page text was checked across the main theory, theorem/derivation appendices, TinyStories 3-gram construction and ablations, semantic-density validation, OLMo experiment, copying exception, and correlation analysis. The four root formulas are reported with their stated idealizations rather than as architecture-independent empirical laws. Primary records were checked for the omitted ambiguity-sensitive MetaHMM paper, Distribution Prompting, two softmax-bottleneck lines, associative-memory scaling, and the contemporaneous empirical-next-token study.
